Amazon **does have a dedicated marketplace in Brazil**—the only South‑American country where it runs a fully local Amazon.com storefront and its own fulfillment network [4]. Outside Brazil, Amazon offers **international shipping through AmazonGlobal**, but there is no local Amazon‑owned logistics or last‑mile delivery in most other South‑American nations [4].  

Amazon has been expanding its presence in the region by **investing in Rappi**, a delivery platform that already services 400 cities across nine Latin‑American countries, giving Amazon an immediate last‑mile network in those markets [5][6]. This partnership is the primary way Amazon reaches customers in countries without its own infrastructure.

Because Amazon’s own delivery footprint is thin, shoppers in places like Argentina, Chile, Peru, Colombia, and others typically turn to **local e‑commerce giants**. The most prominent is **MercadoLibre**, often called “Amazon of Latin America,” which operates its own marketplace and logistics backbone [8]. Other regional players include Brazil’s B2W and Magazine Luiza, and smaller national sites that offer faster, local delivery.

Amazon only runs a fully local marketplace and fulfillment network in **Brazil**; that’s the only South‑American country with an Amazon‑owned delivery system [4]. In every other South‑American nation Amazon ships through **AmazonGlobal**, which does not include Amazon‑owned last‑mile logistics [7].  

To bridge that gap Amazon has invested in **Rappi**, giving it an immediate last‑mile network in 400 cities across **nine Latin‑American countries** (the exact countries are not listed in the sources) [5][6].  

Because Amazon’s own delivery footprint is thin elsewhere, shoppers in Argentina, Chile, Colombia, Peru, and other nations typically turn to local e‑commerce leaders such as **MercadoLibre**—the region’s biggest marketplace that also provides its own delivery services [8].
